The most well known are haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency). Factor XI deficiency, originally called haemophilia C, is mentioned under Inherited Haemorrhagic Disorders, be- low. Haemophilia A (classical haemophilia, factor VIII defi- ciency) is the most common of the serious hereditary bleeding disorders.1 It is an X-linked recessive disorder and therefore, with rare exceptions, males are affected and females are carriers. The condition is due to deficiency of factor VIII and severity of bleeding is related to the resid- ual factor level. The condition is severe when there is less than 1% of normal factor VIII activity, moderate when the factor VIII concentration is 1 to 5% of normal, and mild when the factor concentration is greater than 5%.
